titleStmt.title: Comparison of the triangle and a self-defined two alternative forced choice test
titleStmt.author: McClure
Lawless

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Comparison of the triangle and a self-defined two alternative forced choice test

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The purpose of this study was to provide a direct comparison of a self-defined 2-AFC test to the non-directional triangle procedure.

span.label: sensory discrimination testing
span.quote: The triangle test and the 2-AFC test or paired comparison are commonly used discrimination tests.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Over 600 tests were conducted in both simple and complex food and beverage systems.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: choosing an irrelevant attribute in the self-defined test adds irrelevant variation, which degrades the panellist's later discrimination
span.quote: As shown by the group analysis, choosing a ‘‘wrong” dimension, i.e. attending to some aspect of irrelevant variation, will degrade the subject’s performance.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: wider discriminal dispersion in some subjects makes rank-order reversals (inversions) of the two products more likely, so their responses oppose the majority
span.quote: If the discriminal dispersions are greater for some subjects than others, the possibility of such reversals becomes more likely and thus the choice of a response that is at odds with the ‘‘correct” or majority opinion.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the triangle test requires three implied paired comparisons, whose combined variability lowers its power relative to a directional AFC test
span.quote: Part of the difficulty with the triangle procedure arises from the inherent variability of the three implied paired comparisons that must be performed in order to select the ‘‘odd” or outlying (most different) sample.

span.label: Re-tasting during the preview was permitted but not recorded, so the procedure may have drifted toward a full warm-up protocol for some subjects.
span.quote: Re-tasting was allowed during the preview phase, but was not recorded.

span.label: Variation between the food systems may reflect differences between the judges who happened to participate rather than the methods.
span.quote: As pointed out by one reviewer, some of the variation among the different foods was undoubtedly contributed by differences among judges, as further analysis below will examine.

span.label: Participants were not excluded from later product tests, so the same people could recur across product systems.
span.quote: No attempt was made to exclude earlier participants from a subsequent food product test, although they were of course restricted to participation in only one condition per product.

span.label: The two measures of the same thing disagree in direction: the method with the statistical advantage returns the LOWER estimate of absolute sensory difference, and the paper calls this paradoxical.
span.quote: In summary, the SD-AFC showed a statistical advantage over the triangle procedure in these studies. Paradoxically, the method showed lower absolute discrimination as measured by Thurstonian scale values.

span.label: Below-chance performance was not recorded as below chance: those groups were assigned a d-prime of zero so that the comparison could be run.
span.quote: Groups with performance below chance were assigned a d-prime value of zero for purposes of statistical comparisons.

span.label: What counts as the CORRECT attribute is set by the majority of subjects, not by the manipulation, and a subject can be scored as atypical for disagreeing with the plurality.
span.quote: For all tests, a plurality of subjects used attributes that were similar enough to be grouped. These attributes were categorized as typical. All other subjects were categorized as atypical.

span.label: Who turns up decides part of the result, and the authors say so, crediting a reviewer.
span.quote: As pointed out by one reviewer, some of the variation among the different foods was undoubtedly contributed by differences among judges, as further analysis below will examine. The ‘‘luck of the draw” in terms of who shows up on any given day in a company lab for the day’s discrimination tests may certainly have some effect on the outcome.

span.label: The central question the paper set out to inform is left open.
span.quote: Whether a simple inspection phase is advantageous remains an open question and may depend on the product tested.

span.label: A result relied on in this literature is reported as untested: an overall difference was claimed by taking three non-significant comparisons together, with no test of that claim reported.
span.quote: None of the d-prime values were significantly different when comparing each of the three tests, but ‘‘taken together”, the group with familiarization was reported to have an overall higher d-prime value (no statistical test of that fact was reported, however

span.label: discrimination - as STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE: how reliably a method returns a significant result, on which the SD-AFC beats the triangle
span.quote: Together these results support the suitability of the SD-AFC as an alternative to the triangle test in terms of statistical differentiation.

span.label: discrimination - as ABSOLUTE SENSORY DISTANCE: the Thurstonian d-prime, on which the same SD-AFC comes out LOWER than the triangle for the same products
span.quote: However, when comparing the d-prime values, a different pattern emerged. For the soup, the SD-AFC had a lower d-prime than the triangle (z = 2.04, p < .05) and for the tea, it had a lower d-prime than the triangle with preview

span.label: preview - a single presentation of both test stimuli before testing, explicitly contrasted with the more extensive warm-up
span.quote: A preview sample was defined as a presentation of both test stimuli before beginning the actual testing procedure.

span.label: d-prime - stated here as the Thurstonian measure of sensory difference, and used precisely because it is claimed to allow comparison ACROSS methods
span.quote: Thurstonian distance estimates (d-prime values) allow direct comparisons across different methods for the degree of sensory difference that is perceived.

span.label: inversion - a subject using a relevant attribute but ranking the two products the wrong way round, which the paper distinguishes from choosing an irrelevant attribute
span.quote: Another problem arises when the subject attends to a relevant dimension, but has difficulty rank ordering the stimuli correctly, which we have termed here ‘‘inversion” in our data.

span.label: builds-on → Pfaffmann (1953)
span.quote: Such a testing procedure was mentioned by Pfaffmann in 1953 who discussed both the benefits of incidental warm-up in repeated testing and the possibility of using a personally defined attribute in a two-sample choice test.

span.label: extends → O'Mahony and Goldstein (1986); O'Mahony et al. (1988) warmed-up paired comparison
span.quote: This statement thus foreshadowed the warmed-up paired comparison method of O’Mahony and Goldstein (1986) and O’Mahony et al. (1988) as well as the SD-2-AFC used here.

span.label: contradicts → Angulo et al. (2007)
span.quote: However, examination of the d-prime values shows that the increase in d-prime was not significant (.52–.98 for N = 9, z = 0.56).

span.label: sensory difference —operationalised-as→ d-prime
span.quote: An increase in d-prime, the Thurstonian measure of sensory difference

span.label: preview samples —renamed-across-fields→ familiarization samples
span.quote: Rousseau, Rogeaux, and O’Mahony (1999) showed that preview samples (called familiarization samples) function differently than full warm-up procedures.

span.label: chi-squared
span.quote: The total number correct (zero through four) was tabulated for each panelist and condition, totaled and compared to the chanceexpected numbers correct using v2.

span.label: z-test
span.quote: z-Test comparisons were performed on the d-prime values within each stimulus to determine the relative performance of the testing procedures under the different conditions.

span.label: beta-binomial model
span.quote: The beta binomial model for examining replicated discrimination test data (Bi, 2006; Ennis & Bi, 1998) was also used to analyze those conditions that were not significant by v2.

span.label: effect size (Thurstonian d-prime)
span.quote: Values of d-prime for each condition were obtained from the tables of Ennis (1993).

span.label: variance
span.quote: Variances of the d-prime values were obtained via the B-values from Bi (2006).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: All possible orders were then compared either using t-tests for the two-sample tests (i.e. W–S vs. S–W) or analysis of variance followed by Tukey tests for the six possible orders of the triangles.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: All possible orders were then compared either using t-tests for the two-sample tests (i.e. W–S vs. S–W) or analysis of variance followed by Tukey tests for the six possible orders of the triangles.

span.label: Tukey post hoc test
span.quote: All possible orders were then compared either using t-tests for the two-sample tests (i.e. W–S vs. S–W) or analysis of variance followed by Tukey tests for the six possible orders of the triangles.

span.label: binomial test
span.quote: Table 4 shows the percent correct, binomial p-values and dprimes broken down for each replicate, for the fruit drink system which was the most difficult discrimination.

span.label: The three AFC formats, including the new self-defined 2-AFC, detected the sensory difference more reliably than the triangle test did.
span.quote: The AFC tests (including the SD-2-AFC) performed better than the triangle on a statistical basis.

span.label: Poorer discrimination in the self-defined 2-AFC went with panellists naming the wrong critical attribute or judging the difference in the reverse direction during the inspection phase.
span.quote: Correlates of poorer discrimination with the SD-2-AFC included miss-identification of the critical attribute (as determined by majority response) or reversal of the direction of the difference during the inspection phase.

span.label: Letting panellists preview both samples before a triangle or 2-AFC test brought no measurable benefit.
span.quote: No advantage of adding a preview to the triangle or 2-AFC was observed.

span.label: Although statistically more powerful, the self-defined 2-AFC produced smaller Thurstonian d-prime values than the triangle test, i.e. less absolute sensory differentiation.
span.quote: Paradoxically, the method showed lower absolute discrimination as measured by Thurstonian scale values.

span.label: Panellists who chose the same attribute as the majority reached higher d-prime values than those who chose an atypical attribute, significantly so for the fruit drink.
span.quote: For the fruit drink, subjects with ‘‘typical” responses had higher d-prime values than those with atypical responses (p < .01), and in the other product systems the d-primes were directionally higher but not significantly different.

span.label: Panellists who reversed the majority direction of the attribute (calling the sweeter sample less sweet) discriminated worse than typical non-inverted panellists in the fruit drink and tea.
span.quote: Typical, non-inverted subjects had significantly higher d-prime values that the groups that were inverted, for the fruit drink and the tea (p < .01) and a marginal effect for the orange beverage group (p = 0.0586).

span.label: The attribute a panellist stated during the preview predicted whether that panellist would answer correctly on later trials.
span.quote: Taken together, these results indicate that the stated criterion of a person in the SD-AFC was a predictor of future performance.

span.label: Self-reported confidence after a preview barely predicted subsequent discrimination performance.
span.quote: Confidence was only a modest predictor of performance in the tests with a preview.

span.label: Presentation-order effects appeared only in the orange beverage, where presenting the weaker sample before the stronger one gave more correct 2-AFC answers than the reverse order.
span.quote: For all 2-AFC tests, the order W–S was higher than the order S–W.

span.label: self-defined 2-AFC (SD-2-AFC)
span.quote: This modified procedure we describe as a self-defined 2-AFC (SD-2-AFC).

span.label: preview sample
span.quote: A preview sample was defined as a presentation of both test stimuli before beginning the actual testing procedure.

span.label: typical vs. atypical responder
span.quote: Subjects were classified in groups based on whether their attribute matched the majority in quality and direction (termed ‘‘typical”) or did not (termed ‘‘atypical”).

span.label: inverted responder
span.quote: Individual using attributes that were opposites of the typical attributes (e.g. less sweet describing the sample with added sucrose) were categorized as ‘‘inverted”.

span.label: paradox of the discriminatory nondiscriminators
span.quote: This difference in the test methods is evident in the paradox of the discriminatory nondiscriminators (Byer & Abrams, 1953; Gridgeman, 1970), a finding that some panelists who fail to find the correct answer in a triangle test will nonetheless answer correctly given a 3-AFC task with the same items (e.g. ‘‘choose the strongest sample”).

span.label: discrimination test method (triangle, triangle with preview, 2-AFC, 2-AFC with preview, SD-2-AFC)
span.term: discrimination test method (triangle, triangle with preview, 2-AFC, 2-AFC with preview, SD-2-AFC)
span.quote: Subjects testing simple stimuli were randomly assigned to one of the following five procedures: triangle, triangle with preview, 2-AFC, 2-AFC with preview, or self-defined 2-AFC (SD-2-AFC).

span.label: presence of a preview phase
span.quote: Subjects testing complex stimuli were randomly assigned to one of the following three procedures: triangle, triangle with preview, or SD-2-AFC.

span.label: added sucrose concentration in the fruit drink
span.term: added sucrose concentration in the fruit drink
span.quote: Samples were made at the manufacturer’s recommended concentration (2.1 g mix/1.0 L solution) with 9% or 10% (w/v) sucrose added.

span.label: added monosodium glutamate in the broth
span.term: added monosodium glutamate in the broth
span.quote: Samples were served either with no modifications (control) or with 3.5 g/L commercially available food-grade monosodium glutamate (MSG) added.

span.label: number of correct responses out of four replicates
span.term: number of correct responses out of four replicates
span.quote: The total number correct (zero through four) was tabulated for each panelist and condition, totaled and compared to the chanceexpected numbers correct using v2.

span.label: d-prime (Thurstonian sensory distance)
span.quote: The methods were compared for statistical sensitivity to sensory differences and for d-prime values derived from Thurstonian modeling.

span.label: attribute chosen by the subject (typical / atypical / inverted)
span.term: attribute chosen by the subject (typical / atypical / inverted)
span.quote: For the SD-2-AFC condition, an analysis was developed to determine how the attribute selected by subjects affected their performance.

span.label: self-reported confidence after the preview
span.quote: Subjects indicating they could detect a difference formed one group (termed ‘‘confident”) and were compared to subjects indicating they could not detect a difference (‘‘not confident”).

span.label: one test method per subject per product
span.term: one test method per subject per product
span.quote: Some subjects may have participated in more than one product system over the course of several months, but subjects participated in only one test method (condition) per product, by random assignment.

span.label: product batch (broth commingled before modification)
span.quote: Since enough broth from the same lot could not be acquired, all broth used on a given day was commingled before modifications were made.

span.label: order of sample presentation within a replicate
span.term: order of sample presentation within a replicate
span.quote: Each replicate had a randomized order of presentation.

span.label: Over 600 — number of individual discrimination tests run across the four food systems
span.quote: Over 600 tests were conducted in both simple and complex food and beverage systems.

span.label: 30 to 40 — number of subjects used per testing condition, chosen to match industrial discrimination panels
span.quote: Test conditions used from 30 to 40 subjects, in order to be comparable to normal industrial discrimination panels.

span.label: z = 2.04, p < .05 — size of the deficit in d-prime for the self-defined 2-AFC relative to the triangle in the soup system
span.quote: For the soup, the SD-AFC had a lower d-prime than the triangle (z = 2.04, p < .05) and for the tea, it had a lower d-prime than the triangle with preview (z = 3.01, p < .01).

span.label: v2 = 13.81, p < .05 — chi-squared advantage of the self-defined 2-AFC over the triangle in correct responses for the tea
span.quote: For the tea, the SD-AFC was again higher than the triangle (v2 = 13.81, p < .05).

span.label: 9% or 10% (w/v) — the sucrose levels distinguishing the two fruit-drink samples
span.quote: Samples were made at the manufacturer’s recommended concentration (2.1 g mix/1.0 L solution) with 9% or 10% (w/v) sucrose added.

span.label: 3.5 g/L — monosodium glutamate added to the modified vegetable broth
span.quote: Samples were served either with no modifications (control) or with 3.5 g/L commercially available food-grade monosodium glutamate (MSG) added.

span.label: over 600 — discrimination tests conducted across the four food and beverage systems
span.quote: Over 600 tests were conducted in both simple and complex food and beverage systems.
